Yes, our project spans multiple disciplines, including wet experiments, hardware design, software development and model analysis. The biggest difficulty we have encountered is the communication barrier between ** disciplines. ** For example, after the hardware department designs and produces microflow control chips, it is necessary to use binding proteins for FCS and FCCS testing to verify the function and design logic of the hardware. However, hardware students are not familiar with the instruments and processes of these biological experiments, and the initial progress was not smooth. In order to solve this problem, we have selected a person in charge of each department, who is mainly responsible for communication and coordination. At the same time, in the cooperation between hardware and wetlab, we arranged a wetlab student to deeply participate in the work of hardware, including participating in group meetings and assisting in experimental design and testing. In addition, we insist on holding a regular team meeting once a week, so that in addition to team affairs, each department can share the work, experience and ideas for promoting the project during the week. Through these measures, we have significantly increased the frequency of cross-departmental communication, shortened the distance of collaboration, gradually formed a common language, and really became familiar with each other's work. Finally, we realized that interdisciplinary is not only "collaboration", but also co-creation, which is also the most important lesson taught to us by iGEM.
